overview: Two anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rods with very different clinical niches — soft tissue/foodborne disease versus antibiotic-associated colitis.
genZNote: C. perfringens crashes the wound party. C. diff crashes the gut after antibiotics clear the room.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: An anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod causing gas gangrene (myonecrosis) and food poisoning.
aspects.valueB: An anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod that overgrows after normal gut flora is disrupted, causing antibiotic-associated colitis.

aspects.label: Major Disease
aspects.valueA: Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene), food poisoning, and soft tissue infections.
aspects.valueB: Pseudomembranous colitis, ranging from mild diarrhea to fulminant colitis.

aspects.label: Key Toxins
aspects.valueA: Alpha toxin (a lecithinase/phospholipase C) causing tissue necrosis and hemolysis; also produces an enterotoxin.
aspects.valueB: Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin), which damage colonic epithelium.

aspects.label: Predisposing Factor
aspects.valueA: Traumatic wounds with devitalized tissue and anaerobic conditions, or ingestion of contaminated meat.
aspects.valueB: Recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use disrupting normal colonic flora.

aspects.label: Hemolysis on Blood Agar
aspects.valueA: Double zone of hemolysis (a hallmark finding).
aspects.valueB: Not typically assessed by hemolysis — diagnosis relies on toxin detection (EIA or PCR) rather than routine culture.

aspects.label: Diagnosis
aspects.valueA: Clinical presentation plus wound Gram stain/culture; food poisoning diagnosed via enterotoxin detection in stool.
aspects.valueB: Stool toxin EIA, PCR for toxin genes, or glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen screening.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Causes gas gangrene via alpha toxin; double-zone hemolysis.
aspects.valueB: Causes antibiotic-associated colitis via toxins A/B, following disruption of normal flora.
